newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Crude Outlook - Looking for support from OSPs.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - Looking for support from OSPs.

text.p: Middle East crude differentials could well find support this week, with traders expecting exporters to cut official selling prices (OSPs).
Most Middle East grades have traded at discounts for June-loading barrels, weakened partly by West African imports and seasonally low demand.
But traders said the last round of official selling prices -- at the start of April -- failed to factor in just how weak the market was in view of the potential arbitrage for West African barrels.
The next round of OSPs are expected to be completed this week and traders said they were looking for further cuts in the differential between the OSPs and the Dubai value for the month of April.
If the Dubai differentials narrow, it will support the spot traded differentials.
"Everything depends on where they set the OSPs," a trader with an oil major said. "A good reduction might support the differentials."
The Oman premium to Dubai was cut last month by just five cents to $1.00 per barrel. The result was a slump in spot traded differentials, falling as far as Oman OSP less 22 cents.
For July trading, traders said they expected the Oman OSP to fall at least 20 to 25 cents to bring the crude back into line.
"Everyone knows the differential will come down. If it does not come down at least 20 cents, there will be disappointment," one trader said.
"I don't know that it will affect the June trading left to be done, but it should support July," another trader said.
Light Abu Dhabi grades have been the hardest hit by low demand for June trading, suffering at the hands of West African imports.
Traders said there were still ample supplies of ADNOC grades available for June which would keep prices under pressure.

The Abu Dhabi National Oil Co (ADNOC) cut the OSPs of its key grades over the weekend by $1.75 per barrel. Murban was cut to $18.30, Lower Zakum to $18.35 and Umm Shaif to $18.05 -- reducing their respective differentials to Dubai crude by 28 cents.
Traders said that would help support the price of the grades, but they remained susceptible to competition from West African imports as the Brent/Dubai differential was still narrow.
"When you have alternatives and the alternatives look cheap, then you are under pressure," one trader said.
Trading in most May-loading regional grades is finished, although traders said they were still bearish for Duri crude, suffering from an overhang of supply.
Prompt Tapis has consolidated around quotes plus 40 cents. A producer confirmed it sold a third 600,000-to-650,000-barrel cargo of May-loading Tapis at +40 cents late last week.
